items.title: A vast medieval church emerges from the Sudanese desert
items.summary:
A Sudanese-Polish archaeological team has reached the original floor of what may be the largest church ever built in medieval Christian Africa, uncovering a monumental staircase in the process and raising new questions about the religious geography of a kingdom most of the world has forgotten. The structure, known as the Great Church of Jesus, sits at Old Dongola in northern Sudan — once the capital of the Kingdom of Makuria, a Christian civilization that flourished on the Nile from roughly the 6th century until the 14th. Arabic medieval sources had already identified this building as the largest and wealthiest church in all of Nubia. What archaeologists lacked, until now, was the floor to prove it. Makuria’s Christianity was not a marginal faith. The kingdom converted in the 6th century, likely through Byzantine missionaries, and went on to build churches, monasteries, and monumental public architecture across a desert that the rest of the Christian world Read More… 

A vast medieval church emerges from the Sudanese desert

items.title: Kids already ask AI about God: Here is the question to teach them
items.summary:
A question about God once traveled a short distance. It went to a parent across the dinner table, to a teacher after the bell had rung, to a priest in a parish office on a weekday afternoon. It now travels to a phone at 11 at night and returns in rather less than four seconds, courteous, articulate, and apparently complete. The distance has changed, and so has what happens along the way. The two responses I hear most often from Catholics are of limited use to anyone. One treats the technology as a contagion to be kept from the young. The other treats it as a wonder and leaves the matter there. Neither is much help to a mother whose daughter asked her question hours ago and has had her answer ever since. The real difficulty is narrower than the first response fears and more consequential than the second admits. AI answers about faith sound Read More…

Pope Leo has already officiated at a number of canonizations, but those were all approved by his predecessor. items.title: Pope appeals for peace on Christ the King, dines with Rome’s poor families
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV renewed his appeal for peace around the globe on Sunday, calling on leaders in positions of responsibility to work for equitable solutions to conflicts.

Addressing pilgrims and tourists in St. Peter’s Square for the Angelus on Sunday, the pontiff called the faithful to prayer “for the victims of the many conflicts that, sadly, continue to sow death and suffering throughout the world.”

“Let us pray for those in positions of responsibility,” Leo also said, “that they may commit to finding solutions for reconciliation and peace without delay.”

Pope Leo XIV greets pilgrims and tourists from the window of the Apostolic Palace in the Vatican on Sunday, 22 Nov. 2026. Image ©Vatican Media 

Peace has been a key motif of Leo’s pontificate, and he has prayed for an end to armed conflict in many of the world’s trouble spots, but his appeal this Sunday was global in scope and came on the Solemnity of Christ the King.

In remarks ahead of the traditional noonday Marian devotion, Leo recalled the intention of his predecessor, Pope Pius XI, who established the feast day in 1925, as the world slowly recovered from the horror of World War I.

“ In an era marked by tensions and conflicts,” Leo said, “my predecessor wished to emphasize that the Lord of history is the King of peace and justice for all the peoples of the world.”

“As a pilgrim through the centuries,” the pontiff also said, “the Church renews this teaching, proclaiming that the Kingdom of God is coming and will endure forever.”

Following the Angelus prayer on Sunday, the pope also prayed for young people…
items.t: Pope appeals for peace on Christ the King, dines with Rome’s poor families

items.title: Pope appeals for aid as ‘Super El Niño’ drives severe weather conditions across Asia-Pacific
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV appealed for those suffering from a severe drought across Asia and Oceania, as emergency aid workers continue their work to alleviate conditions of food insecurity and economic hardship.

The U.N.’s Office of Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says the El Niño-driven conditions could compound existing vulnerabilities across vast swathes of the Asia-Pacific region.

OCHA says as many as 190 million children face heightened risks to food and water security, general nutrition and health, as well as shelter, and education.

“My thoughts and prayers go out to the people of Papua New Guinea and other Pacific countries affected by drought,” the pontiff said Sunday after praying the Angelus with pilgrims and tourists gathered in St. Peter’s Square.

All 22 provinces of Papua New Guinea are currently facing emergency drought conditions, while experts are warning that this year’s El Niño phenomenon is driving severe weather across Asia and the Pacific.

The pope expressed his “closeness to all those suffering as a result of this emergency,” and offered his “gratitude to those working to assist the most severely affected.”

The U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization participated in an emergency meeting for Papua New Guinea in late October.

Earlier this month the OCHA issued a forecast saying experts expect humanitarian impacts to unfold in three successive waves over the next six months.

Weather experts say this year’s “Super El Niño” effect driving both drought and severe storm activity.

items.title: The day Bernini’s baldacchino was unveiled at St. Peter’s
items.summary:
On June 29, 1633, the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul, Rome’s patron saints, all eyes are on St. Peter’s Basilica. This morning, workers remove the barriers and scaffolding concealing a gigantic bronze canopy beneath the dome. For the first time, the public can admire Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s baldacchino, commissioned nine years earlier by Pope Urban VIII. The structure is enormous, unlike anything seen before. Crowds flock to the basilica, drawn not only by the reputation of the 34-year-old artist, who is making a name for himself as the Pope’s favorite. The monumental canopy has been the talk of Rome for months. Pope Urban VIII (Maffeo Barberini), who commissioned the work, personally celebrates the feast-day Mass beneath the new canopy. For him, the stakes are enormous. He wants the towering bronze monument, placed exactly above the apostle Peter’s tomb, to proclaim the triumph of the Catholic Church over the Protestant threat. items.title: The only failure is to stop trying
items.summary:
I’m a child of the 90s, a generation that famously celebrated being a bunch of slackers. We all dressed in ill-fitting pants and over-sized plaid t-shirts. It would have been the height of bad taste to put on a polo or pair of khakis that fit. We listened to grunge music that celebrated cynicism, rebellion, and dropping out of “the system.” I remember, in high school, if I actually did my homework during study hall instead of goofing off, I would be mocked as a “try-hard.” At the restaurant where I worked, the dishwashers quietly congratulated each other for doing a bad job. The whole aesthetic was world-weary. In retrospect, it’s odd for a bunch of suburban teenagers with literally no experience of the adult world or any kind of hardship to pose as jaded drop-outs, but such was our era. We were too cool to try. We tried our absolute best to not try, Read More… 

The only failure is to stop trying

items.title: Significant Christ the King “firsts”
items.summary:
The feast day of the last Sunday of the liturgical year is rooted in Scripture, but fairly recently established as a universal feast. Here’s a look at some “firsts” of the feast and its historical context. When Pope Pius XI presented his encyclical “Quas Primas” (In the First) in December 1925, the world was still recovering from post-WWI unrest. The Holy Father had already addressed the related realities of nationalism, political division, class conflict, and family strain in his very first encyclical “Ubi Arcano Dei Consilio” (On the Peace of Christ in the Kingdom of Christ).  “Quas Primas” revisited the earlier document’s themes on the universal authority of Christ, insisting that true peace is only found in sincere submission to him. The Pope also affirmed that Christ needs to reign in hearts in people were to avoid succumbing to the secularism that was taking hold in society.  The proclamation also commemorated the 1,600th anniversary of Read More…

items.title: What to take from “human” as Cambridge Dictionary’s ’26 word of the year
items.summary:
The Cambridge Dictionary has named “human” its word of the year for 2026. “Human” is obviously not a new word, but it is under pressure: people are increasingly uncertain what it refers to, and that uncertainty is showing up in the language. Lexicographer Colin McIntosh, who led the selection, pointed directly at artificial intelligence. AI, he said, is changing how people talk about being human. The rise of compounds like “human-made,” now used to distinguish a person’s work from a machine’s output, is a small but telling sign. When you need an adjective to clarify that something was done by a human being, the category has started to feel less self-evident than it once did. Cambridge’s existing definition of “human” already does some philosophical work: it sets the human against gods, against animals, and against machines. In 2026, that third contrast is the key one. The question of what “human” means has been contested in Read More… 

What to take from “human” as Cambridge Dictionary’s ’26 word of the year

items.title: How the cross is the primary sign of Jesus’ kingship
items.summary:
Whenever we think about kings, we likely imagine a man sitting on a throne, wearing a jeweled crown and long flowing robes. Furthermore, in the United States there remains a cultural aversion to any kind of king, dating back to the very foundations of the country. Kings, in this context, are viewed as greedy rulers who impose unjust taxes and are to be avoided at all costs. It’s interesting, then, that one of Jesus’ main titles is King of the Universe. He does not appear as one of our earthly kings, an unjust ruler who hoards everything, spending it on expensive crowns and comfy thrones. His kingship is quite the opposite. items.summary:
Pope Leo offered a reflection on today’s solemnity before leading the faithful in the midday Angelus. He considered why this feast was established at all and what it means. Here is a translation of his reflection: ~ Dear brothers and sisters, happy Sunday! Today we celebrate the Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe. The Gospel we have just heard presents him to us as the Lord who reveals the true meaning of justice through a dialogue in which everyone is involved — both the righteous and the wicked (cf. Mt 25:31-46). Christ is the measure of justice because he is the author of salvation; by illuminating our relationships, he reveals their truth in himself, in opposition to all forms of corruption. items.title: Have you heard of Catholic doulas for the dying
items.summary:
At the end of life, support can come in many forms: hospice and doctors for medical care, priests to offer Anointing of the Sick, and families to show their love. Recently, many people have hired a new form of help: an end-of-life doula. This unique subset of doulas include Catholics who understand the importance of walking alongside people as they prepare to enter eternal life. Many people may be familiar with the role of a birth doula, a person employed by the expectant mother to help her prepare for birth — before, during and even after labor. Molly de Marcellus, an end-of-life doula in Virginia, points out that there is a connection between these roles. They both assist with a major transition: from the womb to life out in the world, and then from life on earth to eternal life.  Julie Larsen, who trains doulas through a program called Mary’s Embrace, comments, “I think of Read More…

items.title: The four “abortion guys” I met in jail
items.summary:
In 1989, I got arrested for the right to life (and for a girl). A year later I was sentenced to two weeks in a San Francisco county jail.  In between, though, I got confirmed — and it was just in time. Confirmation is supposed to give you “a special strength of the Holy Spirit to spread and defend the faith by word and action as true witnesses of Christ” — and that turned out to be exactly what I needed.  I did my time in an adult work release program rather than a cell. Each day, I reported to a field office and then was assigned to a supervisor to work with in the Golden Gate National Recreation Area. The work was light, so the hardest thing I had to do was admit why I was there — to convicts who didn’t share my pro-life sympathies. First, I met an Anti-Abortion Secularist. I was Read More…

items.title: There’s probably a cult hiding in plain sight on your high street. At last, Britain is confronting the problem | Rachael Reign
items.summary:
As MPs discuss the menace of ‘high-control religious groups’, I welcome the political attention – but survivors of this abuse deserve real action

  • Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

Britain is confronting its cult problem. Better late than never.

They don’t advertise themselves as cults. They don’t register as cults. And they certainly don’t have the word above the door. But make no mistake: cults operate in communities across Britain. Chances are, there’s one on your local high street.

Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org.

items.title: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism
items.summary:
Netflix documentary Primetime Preacher$ travels back to a time when evangelism found a dominant place on US television – and the shocking tabloid stories that followed

For three decades, film-maker Joe Berlinger has gripped true-crime buffs with his deep dives into small-town murders and infamous serial killers. His Netflix explorations of John Wayne Gacy and Jeffrey Dahmer helped flip documentary storytelling from viewer homework to a welcome distraction.

After dedicating so much time to the life of Jeffrey Epstein, the kidnapping of JonBenét Ramsey and other unsolved mysteries, Berlinger thought Primetime Preacher$, his new Netflix documentary on America’s televangelist boom, would offer a break. But it turns out that’s a pretty juicy crime story too, about the religious right’s bank job on American politics. “The deeper resonance for me came when I realized that the global televangelism rise actually mirrors the rise of the religious right,” he says. “Religion and politics, from Reagan on, has really changed politics for the worse in my opinion. This was the birth of that.”

items.title: Early Christian fresco of Jesus found near ancient Nicaea
items.summary:
Archaeologists working near the Turkish town of Iznik have uncovered a rare fresco of Jesus Christ inside a 3rd-century underground tomb: a painting so well-preserved that it is now considered one of the most significant finds in early Christian archaeology in the region. The image, found during excavations at Hisardere Necropolis in August 2025, depicts Jesus as the Good Shepherd: a young, clean-shaven man in a Roman tunic, carrying a goat across his shoulders, surrounded by other animals and flowering vegetation. Lead archaeologist Gülsen Kutbay has described it as possibly the only known example of its kind in Anatolia, the vast historical territory that covers most of modern-day Türkiye. The Good Shepherd was one of the central images of early Christianity. In the decades and centuries before the cross became the universal emblem of Christian faith, it expressed protection, salvation, and divine guidance, drawn directly from the Gospel of John. “I am the good shepherd,” Read More…

items.title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum
items.summary:
In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play

At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash.

Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre.

items.title: Religious messages US agriculture secretary emailed to staff deemed unconstitutional
items.summary:
A federal judge ruled that messages sent by Brooke Rollins to USDA workers suggest Christianity is a shared faith and violate the first amendment

Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday.

Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions.

items.title: US Catholic bishops’ new AI task force urges regulation and worker protections
items.summary:
U.S. Catholic bishops are calling for guardrails on artificial intelligence as the Catholic Church seeks to protect humanity while technology advances.

They are following Pope Leo’s lead, who has said that AI is humanity’s biggest challenge today. His first encyclical, “Magnifica Humanitas”, called for robust AI regulation.

Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, California, emphasized the unique role the U.S. church is well-positioned to play when he addressed his colleagues at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ annual fall gathering Wednesday. From his Silicon Valley diocese, Cantú chairs the conference’s new AI task force focused on preserving human dignity.

“The Church possesses something that Silicon Valley cannot engineer: over 2,000 years of wisdom on the human person, on truth, and on the common good,” Cantú said.

The bishops have been meeting with tech company executives and political leaders to discuss AI, much of which is developed in the U.S. Cantú told the gathering in Baltimore that the task force will help lobby lawmakers for “clear guardrails on the development and use of AI.” The group “will continue monitoring labor impacts and advocating for workers.”

Bishops are particularly concerned about young people’s use of AI. The task force hopes to become a clearinghouse on best practices and AI literacy.

“The Church’s contribution is to insist that every human being possesses inherent dignity that no algorithm can measure and no market can price,” Cantú said.

The bishops also approved updates to their investing guidelines, which are used by other Catholic…
items.t: US Catholic bishops’ new AI task force urges regulation and worker protections

items.title: St. Peter’s Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of the Catholic Church
items.summary:
ROME — St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Catholicism whose commanding dome defines the Roman skyline and is a monument to artistic achievement and perseverance, marked the 400th anniversary of its dedication on Wednesday.

Pope Leo XIV dedicated a Mass “to one of the most celebrated monuments in the world,” telling the faithful gathered beneath the basilica’s soaring vaults that “visiting this majestic church always stirs emotion: We are filled with awe, inspired by the sacredness of faith, the power of history and the beauty of art.”

The Chicago-born pontiff also reflected on the scale of the structure, which stretches roughly the length of two American football fields.

“The vastness of the Vatican Basilica reflects an enduring vocation to welcome, so that as many people as possible may find a place in the church,” Leo said.

St. Peter’s construction spanned 120 years, 20 pontificates and the work of a succession of 12 architects, enduring the Protestant Reformation, which started in 1517, and the Sack of Rome in 1527 before Pope Urban VIII dedicated it on Nov. 18, 1626.

“You walk through those doors and you won’t feel the conflicts and the disasters and the setbacks,” said Elizabeth Lev, a Rome-based American art historian. “You walk through those doors and you see continuity and beauty and achievement and triumph.”

A setting for papal ceremonies and a destination for millions of pilgrims each year, the basilica was built over the traditional burial site of the Apostle Peter, replacing a church that had stood for more than a millennium.

items.t: St. Peter’s Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of the Catholic Church

items.title: Mexico’s Catholic street DJs turn annual Marian pilgrimage into a party
items.summary:
MEXICO CITY — A sea of people carrying statues of Mexico’s patron saint, the Virgin of Guadalupe, marched along the avenue leading up to the country’s most important basilica on Wednesday.

Such pilgrimages are practically embedded in the daily rhythms of the bustling Mexican capital. But the roughly 1,000 pilgrims from across the Latin American nation aren’t just Catholic devotees.

They’re also Mexican street DJs.

The annual procession and street party known as the “sonidero” pilgrimage is perhaps one of the most Mexico City-esque convergences of celebrations to hit the city.

Sonideros, as they’re known, are a particular brand of DJs found primarily in Mexico City, but also in other parts of Mexico and Colombia. The DJs mix rhythmic tunes of cumbia with radio announcements, chanting shout outs that mingle with the music.

The tradition is so important in the city, particularly in working-class neighborhoods, that in 2023 the city government recognized sonidero culture as intangible cultural heritage — a designation UNESCO quickly celebrated. The music has even evolved into its own dance, a derivation of cumbia that has more open steps meant for street parties than the classic two-person cumbia.

Each neighborhood has its own set of sonideros who organize pop-up mobile parties. Wednesday’s party-procession on the avenue leading up to the famed Basilica de Guadalupe wasn’t so spontaneous, but rather part of an annual celebration now spanning decades.

“The root of faith in Mexico is the Virgin of Guadalupe,” said Christian Castañeda, a musician who joined the throngs of…
items.t: Mexico’s Catholic street DJs turn annual pilgrimage into a party

items.title: Pope prays with Irish archbishop and families of the disappeared during ‘The Troubles’
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV met on Wednesday with Ireland’s senior archbishop and the families of people who went missing during The Troubles. 

A period of violent conflict over the question whether Northern Ireland should remain part of the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland, The Troubles unfolded between the late 1960s and the signing of the Good Friday Agreement in 1998.

Archbishop Eamon Martin of Armagh, Primate of All Ireland, joined the pope and family members of 17 people believed to have been abducted, killed and secretly buried during The Troubles by Irish republican paramilitary groups.

After the weekly General Audience on Wednesday, Leo recited a special prayer with the archbishop and family members, asking for the return of the Disappeared.

The bodies of 13 of the 17 have been found, but the remains of four are still missing. 

A fifth person, Lisa Dorrian, disappeared in 2005 and is also considered one of the Disappeared by some campaigners.

Dorrian’s case, however, falls outside the remit of the Independent Commission for the Location of Victims’ Remains, a joint body of the Irish and British governments established in 1999 to find the burial sites of the Disappeared.

“From the bottom of [my] heart I implore anyone with information to please come forward and show mercy so that the remaining families can give their loved ones the dignity of a Christian burial,” Martin said after the meeting.

Violence mainly took place in Northern Ireland, but it spilled over into the Republic of Ireland, England, and even parts of Europe.
